title: RMO — Riemann Map Operator
description:
A bright front moves across the Sun. What is the plasma doing?

A solar flare or a sudden expansion of a coronal mass ejection can set the surrounding plasma into motion. Shocks, expanding regions and moving boundaries may develop together as parts of one connected wave pattern.

RMO — Riemann Map Operator — asks which connections between neighbouring plasma states are compatible with the observations. Density, pressure, plasma flow and magnetic field must change together according to the physical equations. The connections that remain possible form a Riemann map.

Explore the application: RMO QuickLook — rmo-solar.org

QuickLook helps users compare possible explanations, inspect the supporting checks and identify which additional measurement could distinguish them. Start with a supplied model or a published solar event, inspect its inputs, and explore the available results. Model calculations and literature-event reviews are presented separately.

Two ways to use RMO

Online: open rmo-solar.org in your browser. The website provides the QuickLook interface and a hosted Python calculation service. Supported new calculations run on that server; no Python installation or code download is needed. Save your work using the available JSON and PDF downloads.

Locally: download and extract the complete application ZIP from this record or GitHub. Install Python and the supplied dependencies, then start the local Python server and open QuickLook in your browser. The interface and calculations run on your own computer. The README gives the verified Python version and step-by-step commands for Windows, Linux and macOS. Opening the HTML file alone does not start the calculation service.

The current application tests local connections around a selected front within ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD). Results depend on the available measurements, stated assumptions and implemented models. Missing measurements remain unknown. A literature-input review does not by itself determine the observed wave type. Reconstructing an eruption’s complete wave pattern remains a wider goal.

Software version 1.0.0

Saved Fast shock, Slow shock, Contact and Rotation examples are available from QuickLook. Input validation and new calculations are separate actions. Verification covers targeted workflows; it does not establish complete browser coverage, production load capacity, global uniqueness or exhaustive MHD coverage.

This archive contains the application source, presentation assets, documentation, licences and validation records. The scientific data and reproducibility companion are available separately in the R139 scientific archive.

Original RMO code is licensed under Apache-2.0. Third-party materials retain their respective terms and source acknowledgements. SUVI imagery and video retain NOAA SWPC attribution, with Seaton and Darnel (2018) as the scientific reference.
